own.claim: A conditional deferral is one of the warmest investor states: the investor has said yes to a future conversation, and the only work is to meet the condition they named.
own.why: An investor who defers on a named condition has already decided to reconsider; the relationship is open and the path is clear. This is far warmer than a pass with no condition, and warmer than most first-contact silences.

own.claim: Founders often mistake a deferral for a pass and treat it as closed, or mistake it for a live conversation and send updates too often, losing the investor's attention either way.
own.why: The deferral is a third state, neither live nor closed, and it requires a different cadence and a different kind of message. Most founders have not named it as a state and do not know how to work it.

own.claim: When an investor names a condition, write it down in their exact words, and watch for it, not for the investor's reply.
own.why: The investor will not tell you when the condition is met; you must tell them. A condition like 'hit a real milestone' is vague until you define what counts, and the founder must do that work, not the investor.

own.claim: Most founders in a seed round have five to ten investors in a conditional deferral at any time, and these are often the investors who move fastest once the condition is met.
own.why: A deferral is a low-cost way for an investor to stay warm without committing time, and it is also a low-cost way for a founder to keep an investor engaged without chasing them. The investors who defer are often the ones who will move when the round has momentum.
